Flying Tank is an action-packed side-scrolling shooter that successfully blends old-school arcade sensibilities with modern progression systems. Developed and published by Hexage, the game takes place in a future where humanity has lost control of Earth to an overwhelming alien threat. Players assume the role of a mercenary pilot commanding a heavily armed flying combat vehicle, embarking on dangerous missions to push back against the invaders and reclaim what remains of the planet. While the premise is straightforward, it provides enough context to give purpose to the constant stream of battles and destruction that define the experience. The core gameplay revolves around fast-paced aerial combat across a lengthy campaign filled with enemy forces, environmental hazards, mini-bosses, and massive boss encounters. Flying Tank immediately captures the excitement of classic shoot-'em-ups by delivering responsive controls and nonstop action, but it goes beyond simple nostalgia through a well-developed upgrade system. Every mission rewards progress, allowing players to enhance their firepower, unlock new abilities, and gradually transform their vehicle into a devastating war machine. This sense of growth keeps the gameplay engaging and motivates players to continue experimenting with different strategies. One of the game's strongest features is its extensive customization. Rather than limiting players to a single style of play, Flying Tank offers a wide variety of weapons, bombs, drones, and special abilities that can dramatically change how battles unfold. Certain upgrades focus on increasing offensive capabilities, while others improve survivability or utility. Features such as slow-motion combat effects and powerful temporary boosts add another layer of tactical decision-making. Because multiple tanks are available, each equipped with unique special skills, players are encouraged to explore different combinations and discover setups that best suit their preferred approach to combat. Enemy variety also plays a significant role in maintaining the game's momentum. The campaign introduces multiple factions, each bringing distinctive enemy units and attack patterns. As missions progress, encounters become increasingly intense, requiring players to react quickly while carefully managing resources and positioning. Boss fights stand out as some of the most memorable moments in the game. These large-scale battles combine impressive visual design with challenging mechanics, forcing players to learn attack patterns and make effective use of their upgraded arsenal. The escalating difficulty creates a satisfying sense of accomplishment when particularly demanding encounters are finally overcome. Visually, Flying Tank delivers an appealing blend of colorful effects and post-apocalyptic science-fiction aesthetics. The environments showcase a world scarred by war and alien occupation, while explosions, weapon effects, and enemy designs provide constant visual excitement. The artistic direction gives each mission its own identity and helps distinguish the game from many smaller shooters that rely on simpler presentation. The action remains easy to follow despite the chaos on screen, which is essential for a genre built around precision and quick reactions. The sound design complements the gameplay effectively. Powerful weapon effects give combat a satisfying impact, while the energetic soundtrack keeps the pace high throughout the campaign. Music and sound work together to emphasize major moments, particularly during boss encounters and large-scale battles. The result is an audiovisual package that captures the adrenaline-fueled atmosphere expected from a modern arcade shooter. Another welcome addition is the inclusion of cooperative multiplayer. Playing alongside a friend adds extra excitement to missions and makes the campaign even more enjoyable. Cooperative play encourages teamwork while increasing the amount of chaos on screen in the best possible way. The game's accessible controls and straightforward objectives make it easy for both experienced shooter fans and newcomers to jump in together. Flying Tank is not entirely flawless. Some players may find themselves replaying missions to maximize upgrades or unlock additional content, and the overall structure remains rooted in familiar genre conventions. The narrative, while serviceable, takes a back seat to the action and never becomes a major attraction on its own. However, these limitations are relatively minor compared to the game's strengths. The shooting mechanics remain consistently entertaining, and the progression system provides enough variety to keep players invested throughout the campaign. In the end, Flying Tank stands as an impressive modern shooter that respects the foundations of the genre while introducing enough customization and progression to feel contemporary. Its combination of intense combat, rewarding upgrades, strong visual presentation, memorable boss fights, and cooperative gameplay creates an experience that is easy to recommend to fans of arcade action. Whether played for short bursts or extended sessions, it delivers a satisfying blend of challenge and excitement that rarely loses momentum. Rating: 8/10

TLDR; this is a bullet-hell game with great potential and very fun to play. Despite all the cons I mentioned below, it is genuinely enjoyable and if also do, please help the devs with your feedback.Having played all Hexage games to date, I have great confidence in their final version of this game. ENJOY! PROS: - Very smooth control, a bit too smooth even at times - There are plenty of upgrades for weapon types, special abilities, perks to choose from - There are various flying tanks to choose, each with different speed, size, and armor value - the variety of enemy is also pretty nice. You get to see threat both from air and ground enemy - The game is challenging enough; it does not hold your hand much aside from the control instruction. - The game is well coloured. Looks full of life and action - Interesting story premise. Can make us invest more in the characters and perhaps have some more story altering choices. - The difficulty scales naturally at the background. When you are more successful, the opponent you face (even the very same stage you just played) will become more aggressive and pose more challenge. There's still more refining to do, but it's a pretty cool way to do it. CONS AND SUGGESTIONS: - All upgrades should have a better description of what is improved, and by how much when you spend that resources - Aside from armor and speed, all tanks have access to the same weapons and upgrades, which makes little point to really pick different ones. Each tanks should have a unique ability or weapon/equipment that no other tank can have. - When your tank is destroyed, you have a death timer (recovery time) which can last a while if you upgrade your tanks (about 15-20 mins), which is very punishing for players' experience. Also, the death timer does not progress when you close the game so the next time you launch, you will have to wait for the remaining duration. While there is a "black box" upgrade that reduce the downtime, I do not think it is a good design to have in a game. It's closer to a mobile game experience where you pay money to have the downtime removed/shortened. UPDATE: the dev have toned down a bit on the death timer, but it's still pretty long and the timer still persist outside of the game. (I logged in 2 days later, and the remaining duration is still there. It's not too long but I think they should look into it) - Equipment lost on death can be a pretty frustrating mechanic. (and Black Box upgrade reduces it too). You have a decent chance of losing ONE OR MULTIPLE RANDOM weapon/equipment that you invested a lot of resource on when you lose a stage. Combo-ing with the downtime mentioned earlier, it feels extra taxing on mistakes you make. Maybe those who likes challenge enjoy it, but it's not for casual play nor for those who don't want to grind for too long. UPDATE: They have added an easy mode that does not penalize death. You can switch to it anytime, but you cannot revert back to normal mode without resetting the progress. So proceed with care. - You can't sell or swap upgrades at the moment. I see that we can turn the upgrade off but that's it. If you want to pick a different one, you have to "die" so you may hope the equipment lost mechanic hits on the one you wish to drop. - Can't map the keyboard at the moment. Not a big deal with it would be nice to have some control customization. - I crashed quite a bit while playing or clicking around. The game is fun enough that I can overlook it a bit, but I've crashed during the boss stage and earned a lot of resources only to crash and earned nothing. UPDATE: I have no longer crashed for the past 2 weeks. Additional suggestions: - I think the dev can add a counter where we get to see which tank have completed which mission, and add some achievement for 1) completing a mission with all different tanks, 2) completing all mission with one tank That way, no matter how the player choose to play (funnelling everything to a single tank or spread out across many tanks), they are still rewarded in some shape or form.

The game overall is great. however be aware that there is currently about two hours of content and a questionable mechanic where you have to wait 15 minutes after your tank dies to use it again. Overall though it is a great game as always from Hexage. I look forward to the mid to late game warcrimes that appear in almost all of their games.

I've followed Hexage for a while and I've enjoyed their other games, and this one is no exception. It shares a lot of elements with Reaper the Pale Swordsman and at the same time is very different. I think this game is not actually in early access anymore, they're still updating it, but for all intents and purposes the game is complete, so I'm not sure why it's still marked as early access. (they probably explain it somewhere like in their Discord or something) All in all a very fun game, and a real challenge at certain points, the plethora of ship, weapon, and ability options are very fun to explore and figure out what works for your play-style or a particular mission, although I do feel that some of them are definitely better than others and some are worse.

As expected from Hexage. Very good quality and low spec game. About the gameplay, 2d bullet hell . About the controls, i suggest for key binding ,and also an strafe button for maximize movement. About the mechanic , grinding stage as always . But this one is harder than the other games . Quite challenging part. Suggest for an how to play, for starter . Arsenal (garage) - Each ship had it's own arsenal (weapon, bomb, drone , special, upgrades) . 1 primary, 1 secondary, 1 bomb, 2 drone and 6 special(skill) can be equipped at the same time. (*Note : i believed weapons was inspired by Radiant , an retro-shooting game on mobile platform , by Hexage :)) ) - Each category has 6 option except for drone(for now) , for you to chose and BUY . Only after you buy then you can equipped and bring it into the gameplay, And the weapon is spin as a roulette , change each time you COMPLETE ANY mission . That way, you can optimize your BUILDS for your SHIPS. - Mostly equipment can be upgraded to tier 3 with better performance and percentage of effect benefited in the gameplay. - Losing mechanic : After you crashed, destroyed (heath depleted) in a mission, your ship will be repairing in an amount of time , and there's a chance that your ship will loose an EQUIPMENTS (more than 1, even tier 3) . This can be prevented much likely by buying upgrade "Black box". - Disable mechanic : You can turned off any unwanted upgrade or weapon slots ( minimum weapon requirement 1, primary or secondary , bomb doesn't count ). *Remove or selling mechanic : (doesn't have) . This , from what I see is that if you buy whole 6 weapon slots in any category, you can't remove it but only upgrade it . the only way to remove it is by losing (the losing mechanic) for an re-roll of the weapon roulette .I think the dev should add such futures . -Ships : (Currently can be acquired by completing mission) has two stats : health (hit-points) and speed(movement speed) depends on your build to choose an preferred ship . (*Also think the dev should add buying and selling mechanic) Gameplay : - Spin around of shooting the opponents (scavengers and aliens). - Each enemy has an different "Biomass"(Use for upgrading equipment) drop rate , which can be increased by buying upgrade "Biomass detector" . (Notice some of them don't even drop or have an percentage of 1%) -Weapons has cooldown , take caution to gameplay more - Has skill(buy in the garage) help player to pass through difficult scenes. - Varieties boss ( currently 3), and some mini bosses. Story : still in development , chap 1 done. That's for now. Thank you for creating the game . Much love to Hexage.

Update: After investing more time in the game, I definitely don't recomment it. The game's unique mechanic to take away one or more weapons and equipment after each exit from the game (game crash and power outage included) while you're in a mission is opposite of fun. Since this usually involves the best gear you spent hours upgrading, you'll waste a lot of time getting it back to the powerful rank. Also, achievements are broken. Shoot'em-up featuring a lot of action and a lot of equipment to suit all gamestyles. The story is a nice touch and gives your actions some purpose, but it's essentially just another scenario in which aliens invade the world and transform it into a wasteland. The remaining survivors, of which you are a part, is currently attempting to retake the world and simply trying to survive. Presentation is nice because characters talk during different parts of the mission. The options are kept to a minimum. There’s absolutely nothing meaningful in there except for volume. However, this is not a problem because more options would deviate from the game's premise. You are immediately placed on the map when you start the game. Because there are only two ships accessible, entering the garage gives you little options. They are very similar in terms of attacking power. Although weaponry can be classified as primary or secondary, the difference is meaningless because both ships can equip any weapon. The only real difference are random upgrades. These are minor advantages such as faster reloading or extra armor. Of course, you unlock more ships as you play the story. However, you begin with only the most basic weapons and upgrades. Each piece of hardware is upgradeable multiple times. But everything must be purchased using biomass obtained from vanquished enemies. You must work hard for it because simply killing an enemy is not always sufficient. For example, eliminating an opposing vehicle releases a pilot. If you want biomass, you must either smash into it or kill it. If the pilot splatters on the ground, you get nothing. Weapons have infinite ammo, however the chamber can only contain so many rounds. The stronger it is, the less bullets it holds. The weapon recharges automatically, but some only let you to fire one shot before needing to be recharged. Missions are selected from a map and can be replayed. They unlock in the exact order listed, so you don't get to choose which one to play. Difficulty isn't very challenging, but dying can be painful. Aside from losing some of the biomass, you may also lose some of your equipment. This can be excruciating if it has been fully upgraded.

Holy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is TRAAAAAAAAAAAAASH!! From the great minds that brought you the greatness that is "Redcon" comes this pile of smoking trash.. somehow...... When first launched it seems promising but the problem is - on it's first stride it just goes nowhere and falls flat on it's face. You've played first 3 minutes - you've seen it all; And I wish I was joking. In my many an encounter with various games and genres I have rarely (if ever) hit such a specimen. I mean developer seems to not really know what makes schmup a schmup. See if this still feels like something you want to waste your time on (I suggest you don't), because after self-deceiving myuself for ~3 missions, the only thought filling my mind was "just pleeeease let this torture EEEND!". Such is life of a completionist... I'll just list the issues in severity from worst to small-worst: * The levels are absurdly long. Possibly 20 minutes of no-save, no checkpoint trudge. * Levels are barren. It's just a long wallpaper scrolling in the background with no impact or relation to the gameplay. Might as well been a black void in the background. No height differences, no obstacles to avoid, zilch. * Guns suck. The reload system feels retarded and unmitigatable - you just have your guns jam at the worst possible moment with seemingly no fault of your own (see jets'n'guns for a good firepower-limit solution devs); some gun combos shoot together, others don't. Because consistency. And all weapons essentially feel the same. * You know how every game nowadays has the meta-progression: you die, you get to keep some cash, you upgrade, you come back stronger. Same here? Hell no! Some genius came up with the idea of reverse progression - you die, you loose some part of your upgrade sub-system. Sounds fun? Fk no! * Enemies are repetitive. No interesting attack patterns. And they all look kinda the same. * The UI is clunky as hell. It's recommended to play with a controller, but boy oh buy, good luck navigating the confusing layout and bass-ackwards button mappings in game and menus (not remappable. of course. Why? Would expect to be able to? pfffft, frking weirdo.) * Enemy waves are uneven. There are moments where you are swarmed with enemies and then for no reason it's 20-30s of nothing, just slowly flying forward. * Music kinda sucks and is repetitive af, there's probably like 2-3tracks max. Which is fun, when as I'vementiond - mission length is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane. * Generally it's mostly unchallenging. * Story generic and uninspired. Ending was an exposition dump which was like.. who even does that?! People tend to not know how to wrap up their stories, and just finish abruptly with "lived happily ever after". Here "lived happily ever after" feels like a history tractate - mostly stuff having nothing to do with anything. * and so on and forth.. but I'm vented and bored now, and so are you. Good things? Dunno. It looks nice. Not "OMG-it's-so-beautiful". Just nice. Pleasing to the eye.
